files_reviewed: .env.local.example (key names only; values are blank placeholders except a placeholder base URL)
README.md (security and architecture sections, grep for the rest)
note: Next.js app on Cognee Cloud (answers and memory) with a Groq router that picks one configured webhook action per turn. No SQL database: Upstash Redis and one shared Cognee tenant, both used server-side only. No model call or model key in browser code. No committed secrets. Real controls exist: Google sign-in plus per-route membership checks on /api/companies/*, SSRF checks on webhooks at connect time, HMAC-signed payloads, action caps (5 per customer per hour, 100 per company per day), a 60 s dedupe, at most one tool call per turn, and server-side re-validation of tool args by type. The main gaps are customer identity taken from the request body, cross-company session reads through the shared tenant, no rate limit on the public chat endpoint, and model-fired webhooks with no confirmation step.

labels.what: Customer identity comes straight from the request body. visitorId and email are not verified, and customerId is a hash of the email. Anyone with the public widget key can send a victim's email. They then get that customer's remembered history in answers, write into their memory, and fire webhook actions (for example a refund ticket) in the victim's name.

The conversation detail page loads any session id from the URL with sessionDetail. It never checks that the id starts with everdesk-<slug>-. All companies share one Cognee tenant, so a member of company A can read company B's transcripts. The layout only checks membership of slug A.

The feedback endpoint takes any sessionId from the body and does not scope it to the caller's company. A member of one company can write feedback entries into another company's session in the shared Cognee tenant.

A client-supplied sessionId is accepted when it starts with everdesk-<slug>-. The id is never tied to the visitor, so a caller who knows or guesses another customer's session id (slug, 8-hex customer hash, timestamp) can append to that session and draw on its session context.

Membership for all dashboard pages is checked only in the shared layout. The page components (settings with public key and member list, actions, customers, conversations, overview) read data by slug with no check of their own. The proxy only checks that a user is signed in. Next.js does not re-run layout checks on every segment request, but the README claims every page enforces membership per request.

The Groq router picks an action and the server POSTs the webhook in the same request. Actions are described as refunds, tickets and escalations. Neither the customer nor staff confirms before it fires. The only checks are rate caps and dedupe.

The router prompt says to take parameter values ONLY from the customer's message and never invent them. validateArgs checks only type, length and magnitude. Nothing checks that a value appears in the message. The landing FAQ (src/app/page.tsx line 94) depends on this rule when it says the agent never invents an action or its parameters.

The rule that customer text, the answer and history are DATA, never instructions, exists only in the prompt. The code puts the raw message, answer and history inside triple-quote delimiters without escaping, so a message that contains triple quotes can break out of the data block.

The prompt says to call a tool only when the customer's message clearly matches and to call nothing when in doubt. Code fires any tool call the model returns. The grounded flag goes to the model, but no code checks it, and no confidence or confirmation gate exists.

The system prompt says to answer ONLY from context and never invent order numbers, dates or events. Code has no groundedness check. pickAnswer drops answers that match a refusal regex and then picks the longest one.

Number params from the model are accepted up to 1e15 and strings up to 500 chars. An action config has no min, max or allowed-value setting, so a refund amount or similar money field has no business limit before the webhook fires. Rate caps exist, but values are not bounded.

The public chat endpoint has no rate limit per IP, key or visitor. Each call runs a paid Cognee recall with an LLM completion, a durable memory write with cognify, and Redis writes for a new visitor. Only the Groq router has a budget.
Access-Control-Allow-Origin * on the chat endpoint, so any site can call it with a scraped public key.

The customer message is stored word for word in durable memory. Later that history is appended to the system prompt, and the new message is joined into the query with no injection guard. This allows stored prompt injection, and the answer path has no data-not-instructions framing.

The per-customer cap of 5 actions per hour is keyed on customerId, which comes from the client's visitorId or email. Rotating visitorId bypasses it. Only the 100-per-day company cap holds, and an attacker can use it up to block real customers' actions.

Training URL fetch checks DNS once and then uses fetch with redirect: follow. A public URL can redirect to an internal or metadata address, and DNS rebinding is not blocked. The blocklist misses ranges that webhook.ts blocks, such as 100.64/10 and most IPv6-mapped forms. The fetched text goes into the knowledge base, where the agent can read it back. webhook.ts line 17-18 notes that training fetches tolerate redirects.
The whole response body is read into memory before the 2 MB size check runs.

Forget deletes every memory item whose filename contains the URL id, a plain substring match on an id that is never validated. An id such as txt or cust_ matches every item, so any member (not only the owner) can wipe the whole customer-memory dataset in one request.
Uploads have no size, count or type limit, and training (cognify, paid LLM processing) has no rate limit. Any signed-in Google user can create a company and start unlimited training runs.

The overview shows sessionStats from the shared Cognee tenant as Workspace spend and Tokens processed. These numbers cover every company on the tenant, so each customer company sees platform-wide spend and usage.
visitorId (the only credential for an anonymous customer's memory) and the email are stored in localStorage, readable by any script on the widget origin.
/widget sends frame-ancestors *, so any site can frame the chat. This allows clickjacking of the email form and chat. It is intended for embedding.
customerId keeps only 8 hex chars (32 bits) of a sha256, so different customers can collide and share one memory history as the customer count grows.

The resolve form fills in the last customer question and answer by default, and submitting writes them into the shared knowledge base that every customer can retrieve. Customer-specific details can leak to other customers.

All companies share one Cognee tenant and API key. Sessions are not stored per company. Isolation is a session-id prefix filter in app code over the last 200 tenant-wide sessions. The README's isolated-per-company claim holds for datasets, not for sessions.

If listing the memory items fails, the error is swallowed as an empty list and the route still returns forgotten with 0 deleted. The UI then says the agent provably knows nothing. Session transcripts and knowledge-base resolutions that hold the customer's text are never deleted.
After 60 polls (4 minutes) the loop ends even if the graph is not built. It marks the step done and shows Your support agent is live and trained.
Polling shows Training complete. Your agent knows this now once training is false. It ignores the errored flag that GET /train returns, so a failed build is reported as success.
Shows feedback sent before the request and never checks res.ok. A 4xx or 5xx response still shows as sent. Only a network exception resets it.

A hardcoded FEED_LINES event log plays on the landing page under a pulsing live dot as cognee memory ops. A comment and a subtitle say it comes from a real 2026-07-04 session, but it is static marketing data.

Action caps are hardcoded constants: 5 per visitor per hour, 100 per company per day, 500 router calls per company and 10,000 global per day, plus the 60 s dedupe at line 306. The same numbers are written again in docs page text and the README, which can drift.
Groq URL, primary and fallback model names, 4 s timeout and 500-char param cap are hardcoded.

The chat route accepts messages up to 4000 chars, but the router truncates the message to 2000 chars. These are two different limits for the same value, so action params near the end of a long message never reach the router.
The client hardcodes the 10-field limit (params.length < 10) separately from MAX_PARAMS_PER_ACTION.
The embed snippet origin falls back to the hardcoded production domain everdesk.allensaji.dev.
SITE_URL is hardcoded to everdesk.allensaji.dev. The same domain is hardcoded in the webhook and fetch user-agent strings (webhook.ts line 191, fetch-docs.ts line 88) and in opengraph-image.tsx.
Install snippets hardcode https://everdesk.allensaji.dev for the embed script, chat API and widget iframe.
Docs examples hardcode https://everdesk.allensaji.dev. The Forget API is documented for a company backend, but the route requires a dashboard Google session.
Test script hardcodes http://localhost:3000 and the slug zenith-test. It calls dashboard API routes with no auth, so it no longer works with the current membership checks.

The company public key (pk_...) is sent from the browser and printed in the embed snippet. It is publishable by design, but it is the only gate on the chat endpoint that reads customer memory and fires actions.
